segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Anna Gleason Utt was born in 1906 in Spangle. Her mother's parents, the Fricks, were one of the founders of that town and ran the hotel. On this tape, Anna Utt describes the Spangle Hotel, the move to Harvard, and life at home. Different events from her childhood and the work day of her parents are recalled.

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: There… okay.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Should we just sit down?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Okay.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: That orange cup's mine.

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Okay.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: You want to sit down? It doesn't matter. I'm going to end up asking some questions about some folks and stuff that you've actually already told me about. But I wanted you and all of our activity or not. Well, anything will take the streets. I wanted to ask you about your grandparents again. You talked about the ones who lived near Walla Walla, Birdwalla.

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: I don't know my mother's people. I lived at Spangle. They're real old-timers. They were just about built on town, my grandpa and his son, George. I think they were the second people there. Later, they built a big hotel and run that for years and years. Most of their kids were born there, but not all of them. Anyway, they had to go to Walla Walla and haul their stuff back. It was a flower and stuff.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: When was it that they moved to Spangle?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: I have to get some paper on the other.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: 1886 would that be when they moved there? Because that's when their first child was born in Spangle. First...

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Oh, yes. That's between the death of one and the birth of the other. Is that a bricks or a... I can't see it.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: That's a Gleason.

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Oh, that's a Gleason. I haven't gotten it. I can't talk. I can't remember.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: What was the story about the children of theirs that died when they were living in Walla Walla?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Yeah, they died on that. I wish I could find... And then, you know, they couldn't stay there anymore, losing their children that way. So they gave their land to someone that would keep the graves up of the children that died. And they just pulled out and then come to Spangle.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Was there any town there at all when they moved there?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Yeah, there was a man living there by the name of Spangle.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Oh.

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Now, isn't that funny?

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: I have, you gave me some stuff last time about that.

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Right.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Well, we can get them later. Who stayed in that hotel that they ran? What kind of hotel was that?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: It was a big one. I don't know how many stories it was. But Grandpa and Grandma were running as long as they had enough girls. And Grandpa lived. I don't think... Yes, she had to have it quite a while after he was gone. Because he died when my oldest brother was a baby. So that would have to be in 19... 2... 19... 1 or 19... 2. Grandpa was still running when I was a big kid, 12 years old. And of course, Mama worked in there all the time. She was at home. Quite a while afterwards because my folks lived there then until 19... 11. Guess that's when we came out here. I have one or two platters that they used in that hotel. You know, breakfast platters. Big, heavy, thick things. Imagine girls carrying them around.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Did they eat all in one room? Did they feed every one at once?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Yeah, in one big, big room.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: And all the girls helped out for you?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Well, you know, as one would marry off, then another one would probably help out. And... I don't know. They didn't have the hotel when the youngest girl was growing up. She's dead now too. They're all gone except Mama. He was quite a big family.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: There were 12, right?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: No, Mama had 12. I just don't have them. Seems like it was 10. But I can't find them.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Did your father live in Spangle?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Yeah, his parents lived in Spokane at the time, I think. Because my Grandma Gleason was a Gleason in Spokane. And my Grandma Gleason died in 1904. And he lived up there all that time. But my Dad, at that time, was working on farms, I think. Just here and there. And he let people in Spangle go into the hotel and eat. He had the best apple tree there ever was on that. Next to that. And I never found it since. Of course, I wouldn't know it if I did, but it seems like it. It was so delicious that if I ever could find them, I didn't know what was inside the taste of them. It wasn't a big apple, but it was just... You bite into it, the juices run down your chin. I don't know what. It was a summer apple. And they didn't pick them. They just let the kids run to them, you know. And that was some apple tree. And then back of the hotel was their home. It's gone too. But where the highway is going up through Spangle, Spokane, that highway is right on top of it. Where the hotel would have been if the town was still. You know, the high town was more of a curve there then, you know, and the road was down a little bit. But they, uh, they must have gone down. Mama tells me about the big shade trees. Oh, they were huge. Out in front of the hotel, I remember them. And one time, I think she used to call those the salesmen. Come here and sell stuff. But stay at the hotel, you know. One day she was out there and he was picking those long ants off the tree, you know, and pulling the heads off of them and eating their eggs. And he just, um, just loved them. But, you know, even though she was grown, she still shed her wings. And that man eating ants was a big ants. It's a little hard to throw the head away with the rest.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: That's a delicacy now, chocolate covered ants.

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: I know it is... Done that and she couldn't.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Oh, personally, I've never tried any.

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: No, I haven't either, but I suppose if you fell lost in the woods, you could get by with a lot of things you don't think you need.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: They might have saved his life one time, eating ants. Did your parents stay in Spain? Until you were...

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Well, they stayed there until 1911. Then we can load it up like they had. They had a farm, but then they had a farm sale. And I've got that sale bill yet. And they sold out and loaded up kids. They had to have a stall or two, you know.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Did they run the hotel when they stayed in Spain?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: No, no… no, Dad carried mail for years. And then he, you know, one horse buggy and all. And then he worked in the warehouse. The house that we lived in was up here and the warehouse was just down below just a little ways. He'd be running from dinner and lunch and stuff. And then he worked there a while. And then they got on a farm and they lived on that until he sold it to come out here. But up that creek was all friends from Spain. I guess that's why we followed him out. We got here in November, lived in a chicken house. It was on a place down below us, a quarter, no, three-fourths of a mile down. And it was pretty big, full of shit, you know. And then by the next winter, my dad had the log cabin built.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Did he build it himself?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Well, he did most of the work, you know. He had to have, he had someone help, I think, with raising the rafters or something like that. Otherwise... I love that old house. It wasn't much of a...

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: What was it like, the old house?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: I think I have a picture I can show you pretty quick. I got a book like this I kept under. That was my grandma's house. I mean, grandma's break, the one around the hotel. That's that one's from Have a Birthday Sunday. There's one side of it. It's another side of it. Later, I think they built a cellar on out from here for vegetables and fruit and stuff.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Did it have, did the upstairs, did you live in it too?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Yes.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Is that where you neatly slept?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Yeah, that's where all of us kids slept. It was nice. That window on this end is where the coyotes came right up around the house, you know, and they get up and watch them out on moonlight nights, you know.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: They come up very close?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Yeah, they come right up to the, just right up there. Most of these pictures are long, you know, and... That's the oldest boy. He retired a long time ago, of course. That was when he was a banker and a health care worker. And then he left his Spokane bank and he retired.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: How big a house was that that they built? How big was it on the inside?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: It had three rooms in it. It had a big living room and not so big bedroom, but the bedroom was a long one, but not any wider than the beds, much wider, you know, wide enough to get around. And they had three beds in that downstairs and the rest of the beds were upstairs. And then the kitchen was about like that too. A little bit bigger, you know, we had to have a big table. And then they had a bench on one side of the table. Dad always called that the crater roll because all the kids started low and lined up, you know, like that. He'd sit on this end and Mama sat next to him there. And the rest of us was lined up. And it was beautiful. I mean, you know, we had so much fun. And now we never see each other. This summer I saw two of the boys. Oh, man, that was nice. One of them is never, the other one has been in Alaska until he retired. He moved out of Montana and I had to see both of those. And just my sister here. And we don't see each other very often. We talk on the phone. But that's the funniest family.

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: And we just don't get together. And I would like to see them.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: You were all pretty close with them?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Yes… we just always had a family reunion, you know, on something, once a year. Sometimes it was Thanksgiving, but that really was too late, you know, for some of them to come. Sometimes earlier, sometimes we'd go up to Grizzled Camp, have a reunion up there. You know, it was just so much fun.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Do you remember what it was like living in that chicken coop that first winter? Is that pretty hard? Because it must not have been too insulated.

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: No, I don't… i don't remember too much. I remember since we didn't have too much furniture yet, you know, and everything, we weren't too crowded. But they had a tall box. It was taller than that. And the longer... I imagine it was about as wide. And on that wall, they hung their coats. And the little kids, you know, would be back over there and so on, you know. I remember some of the school kids came up to... The schoolhouse was just here, we were here. And some of the girls came up and asked me to come out. But at recess time, I hadn't started school yet. And so I climbed up on that box to get my coat, because I was showing off more than anything else. And then I jumped off. And it killed me, so I remember doing that. Just as plain as... The silly things you do, you always remember. I remember... We didn't, you know, go to the neighbors and stay all night. My kids do not age too much. We could play a little bit in the daytime, but we always had to be home at night. I don't think I ever stayed all night with one of my friends. That was just something that I didn't believe in, I guess. You want to leave the kids home.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Would you usually be home by dinner time? Or would you eat dinner at a friend's house sometimes?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Well, at the new meal we could, but in the evening we had to be home. We could lunch with someone, you know. And he wanted his lunch there. And he used to worry when we got old enough to go out. He didn't care for that too much. But... It was a good time we had at home. But Ruby now, I see her. I hope. What did your family do anything for...

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: What would you do when you were all together in the evenings?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: If it was good weather, of course, we were out. I didn't go too much because, you know, I was the oldest girl and Mama needed help so much. But enough of them to play games, get up to baseball, match, or play run, cheap run. Just enough of them to do things like that.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Was your father playing with them too?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Yeah, he always played ball with us. But baseball... In the wintertime, we crocheted or he would read to us nights a lot. Before electricity, he'd get back up to the little lamps we had, kerosene lamps. And he could read, you know, everybody. Every man would get to those evenings. Especially when a... I guess a side of a farmer would come in. He even kept all the stuff in there. All the stories and stuff in there.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: How often did that come?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: I think just once a month, I think. But maybe it was more. And I don't know. I just don't know.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: What kind of stories would they be?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Oh, I remember one of them. We just thought he could read that so well. It was one of Zane Gray's stories. Man of the Forest, I think. Any story that come out. And then we took a spokesman or a viewer or something. Chronicle, I think it was. And twice a week.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Would he read you the paper?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: If it was good news, you know. I mean, he was up in the news that way.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Would he read you the stories over and over again? If you read out to anyone?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Well, you know, if we put up too big a racket, he would. But he liked to read and he liked to listen. People can get by and do pressure for hard times than anything else. He always had enough to eat… nowadays it's different… kids have to be entertained away from home. And that's sad. I guess. Because kids not age. I have some greatest grandkids. But they grew up so fast.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: What do you mean by that? That they grew up fast?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Well, it seemed like the oldest one, he's 20, he's married now. Liz and Clarkston. And the second one goes to Lewis and Clark and Lewis. College down there. And the third one now is a senior. In potlice. It just seems like we haven't got time for him to grow up that fast. Once a sophomore and yet he's a freshman. And you know they're so busy. School activities just keep them so busy.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Do you think that when you're growing up you have more time to play and fool around with kids too?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Well, you know, things were so different. You know, like in all the days we used to have recesses. 15 minute recesses. And you'd get out and play. And then the game would continue somewhere it left off. You know, the next recess we'd have an hour noon. Well, not always. Not every winter you'd have an hour noon. But you know, it seemed like there was so much time to play. Now they don't have that in school. They have the sports and lots of things and all the kids occupied. And I guess it's better. They seem to be smarter than we were by far. I think it's better to play football.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Were you pretty close to the sisters and brothers in your family that were about your age? Did you have good friends outside of your family?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Well, yeah, I had some friends alright that we chummed with. Only at school. When school was out then that was it. I had some very good friends. I had one living in California. She couldn't get up this summer though. Donna stopped. And I think I got a nice summer. When she passed I guess it was summer. And I saw her sister. Yes, you are. She was here for the first time. I guess 40 years. Maybe not that long. And maybe yes it is. You can't expect so much when you get older. They drive them to be home, you know, like those fabulous dodge homes. Big rugs and complete home. When they come up they drive back. That's what you know Ben.. over in Troy, his sister. She named Dennis. They started in on just making a little bit of wood. And they hauled it out and sold it. Then they made more and hauled it out and sold it.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: They had a small sauna?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: No. They just get a cordon of wood wherever they could pick it up. Maybe on the coast or. And then they got such a big business they needed two trucks. And they kept on going and kept on going until they had a fleet of trucks. And hauling everything for everybody. They made all that good. The boys still in the business. That's what they did to make that money.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: What would breakfast be like? Did you...

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: In my family, Dad got up first. He built the fire, he got it warm.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: When would he get up? How early? Do you know?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Well, then I suppose it was... Oh, it must have been 5:30. Maybe earlier. And he made the coffee and cooked the oatmeal. And he always cooked the oatmeal. The kids always ate it. And I can just stay on my oatmeal. For a little bit. And then all the rest of you would get up. And then he'd yell. And we'd better get up. Let us up, you know. It wouldn't take long to... Whatever it was we had, you know. And get ready for school and be gone.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Did you have any chores there on the house you had to do before you left in the morning? Where did you go to the house?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: I don't think so. Just help me. I have to help the others get ready to go. But I can't remember waiting to wash dishes or anything like that. I suppose Mama does those all after.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Would you come home for lunch?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: No. But that's the job we had to do at 6 o 'clock. That was quite a job, too. For 12 kids. Yeah, you know. We always... Mama baked bread every day. So we always had fresh bread.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: How many loaves would she bake?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: She baked..… i think it was five. I think in the big pan, she had three loaves in the big pan. And two loaves in a smaller pan. That's all her oven would hold. And that's what she baked every day. And if she ran out, she would bake biscuits. And her roof would separate. And save the bread for lunches the next day. Because she got caught up in that. But most often, she would just bake bread. Every day. Every day.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Did you have much white flour that you used? Did you have much white flour? Or was it all whole wheat that she used?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Well, no. We had lots of white flour. You know, you take your wheat de puce and have it ground up. Bring it back home for the winter. Then they get five gallons of honey.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: They get five gallons?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: And the whole model would come way up in the hundreds. She'd come 150 corn bollaries to bake. And she'd come everything. They had their own meat, you know, after we got started. And they were good.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Did you have a cow for milk? And chickens?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Yes. No, I mean, not so many. Well, they were milking too many when they got older. But they just had three or four. Butter and milk and cottage cheese. But, they'd butcher pigs in the fall. Sometimes but not too often. When I was little, they had more beef than when I got older. It was easier for Dad to butcher a pig. Nice and sneaky, but you'd need to run the knife into his finger under the nut. More and more. More and more. And he suffered with that bone and then walked the floor and everything else. Already decided to have his finger taken off.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: How did you preserve the pig? Did you smoke most of it?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Yeah. And we had a smokehouse, you know. We'd smoke in there with the fire bone. That usually was John's job.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: How long would it smoke before it was smoked?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: I can't remember.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Do you have any idea how long? I don't.

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: It seemed like forever, you know, when you're a kid. But I suppose now it would be like everything else. When you're a kid the hills are steeper and the trees are bigger and thicker. The snow is deeper. And when you get old, why it just...

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Had much of the timber...

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: This is my son… what's your name?

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Laura. Laura. Laura Schrager.

segments.speaker: Unknown Speaker
segments.words: How are you, friend… really good… you?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Yeah, we're fine.

segments.speaker: Unknown Speaker
segments.words: You record her for posterity, huh?

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Yeah, exactly.

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: She's putting things down there I say.

segments.speaker: Unknown Speaker
segments.words: Uh oh. Uh oh. Profanity and everything.

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: No, I don't think I've said anything like that, but I may have.

segments.speaker: Unknown Speaker
segments.words: How you been?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: A little bit extra to go, how have you been?

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Where did you work for?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: I worked for Elsie first and then... I was the store manager when I was in the alley. And...

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Did you work in the store?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: No, just a couple of days when they were having a sale or something like that I did. But I just... His house, you know, worked for his wife and took care of the kids. I earned my board that way. Washes were their names.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Did your mother have a routine for what things she did on a certain day? I mean, would she always wash on Monday? Did she have a routine like that to you?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Well, she had to wash two times a week. I remember she washed on Saturday. And I suppose the other day was Tuesday or something like that. Because after Sunday she needed to clean up, you know, and do more business for the week's school lunches and stuff.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Was Sunday a day of rest for you?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Would you work much on Sunday?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Not too often much. We always spent the morning going to Sunday school. I don't think we ever missed that. But then we'd go home to our Sunday dinner. And no, that wasn't much of a work day. It was for mama because she darned and sewed and patched and stuff like that while she was just sitting in the corner. I do those things, you know. And that was the company.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Did most kids go to Sunday school?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Yeah. I can't remember John and Virgil. But I went and little kids went. I don't know how little. They quit.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Did kids from the families around you help most of them?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Yeah, I think so. If I had my own book like this I could show you some of the Sunday school classes. One time Mrs. Moore had a Sunday school class. I just don't know how many was in that, but there was a whole big bunch. We were growing up then. Imagine we were 14, 15, 16. Some of the oldest parents in that class would be 18, 19. Maybe older. But we're young people. Have a son.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Do you remember what you used to do much in Sunday school? What? Do you remember what you used to do in Sunday school much?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Oh, we just each, you know, the classes were all divided. You had to go in there and learn your verses and study the list. That was the sign. You know, you get those. You know. We had to study those and know our list by that time. It was a nice time. There was one, Sal, Silver Moore. We always had to quote a verse from the Bible and he always, his verse was Jesus wept and he would say that every time. And on Friday nights there was,… um, I think it was, I think it was,… oh, you know where everybody meets and they had plays and programs and...

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Literary? It wasn't?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Yeah, literary. I lost that word for a while. Yeah, and that was nice. That was fun.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: What were they like?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: I remember they had a master or a leader or something each time. I just about forgot that. That was on Friday nights.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: They had song?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Songs. People speak pieces or tell stories or... And it was always fun.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Was that just, those were in the schools, weren't they? Was it just the families whose kids who went to school there would come down?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Yeah, well, anybody… it must have been everybody was welcome because I remember older people, I mean, you know, young people but they were too old, much too old for school.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Do you remember any of the debates? Did they have debates?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: No, I don't. That was a long time ago.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: No?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Not right now. Sometimes you can think once in a while, you know, you can go back and think of things that happened then. Some special program or something. If you think of anything like that, you should scribble it down and then when I come back, I don't know whether you'll remember. That would be great. Because not many people, most people have very hazy memories, literally, of specific things that would happen. They sound like they were pretty fun. And then of course up there they had their ladies' aid and they had their sewing, quilting, all of that.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Did you go to that as a kid?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Maybe just a little bit.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Would your mother go to that?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Sometimes, when she had mine. I think that's amazing. I think they're making more stuff there for one of the wars, you know, bandages or I don't know what you're into. But they have been, I don't know how that is.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: How did news of the war affect people around here? Did it mean much to them, the war, the Roam Roam?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: World War I, I can't remember when it was over with. And I remember folks worrying about it. But otherwise, you know, I can't remember the impression of that very much. I would be 18 or 19. I would be 12 or 13. Then the 12 or 13 year old wasn't. You know you don't have TV to watch and you couldn't keep up on the news like you do today. And then the folks never, what it worked was to dwell on it. We always had enough to eat. So I guess that's all kids are interested in really.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Did the girls stay more home than the boys did in your family?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Well, I left when it was time to go to high school. But Betty didn't graduate from high school. She had all the bad eyes at that time. And so she didn't go on. She took music lessons. And she kept up on her music beautifully. Now she teaches music lessons for the last 50 years or so.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: What does she play, piano?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Piano. She has a nordic. She's good on that. She gives music lessons. Maybe 15 a week or something. That don't sound like much. Kids go to school, you know, and they have to come mornings and evenings.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: You left home right when you graduated from eighth grade? Right after that?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Yeah, right afterward. And I went down to potlatch. The first one I worked for was Dr. Thompson. His wife. In the home. I loved that place to work.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Were you expected to do very much?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Well, not there. I was kept busy in the morning. And then after I got my new dishes done, then I was expected to rest. Even though I didn't care for that. I didn't get about having to rest and have, you know. But then when the evening meal was time for that, I was asked to get up and go to work again.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: When did you go to school?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: I worked for them in the summer. Then when school started, I went to Elsie's. Just Elsie's. And stayed there on my board. That was a beautiful place to stay too. They were a favorite subject to us.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: So you never lived at home again after eighth grade?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Yes, I did. We came home then in fall of 23 maybe. And then we walked from Princeton. Well, last time at school. Until I graduated. I was home then.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: What, you told me a story last time about when your mother got sick at one point. And she wanted you to come home and quit high school, too?. You know. Was it important to your folks for you to go to high school? For the kids to go to high school?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Well, it seemed to me. I know they tried awful hard to keep all of them in school. The boys, you know, then didn't care much about high school. They didn't think that that was all that necessary. They had been getting along a long time without going to high school. So they kind of walked on it.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: But your parents encouraged them to go?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Yes… my dad got a Ford finally. And let the boys take that to school, you know, so they wouldn't have to walk. That was quite a bit later after I graduated. But they somehow get up to the junior year and then they would quit, except the last two younger ones. They finished. The other, see there would be Brendan, Mark, Claud. I don't know. Yeah, I think that they all quit junior year.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Were they anxious to get out and make the almighty dollar?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: No, they didn't care. That was the thing. It wasn't so hard. They had to find work, you know. School doesn't mean so much. It didn't, I mean. Now, they not only have to have high school, they have to have college. And that's nice. You get old fast enough anyway without, you know, starting to work when you're a kid.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Did the girls in general, were they more interested in school than the kids? Was that true for more families than just yours?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: I think it was true, you know. It seemed like I can remember a lot of boys that didn't know, I mean, graduate. Okay. Well, I know. What would, because we talked about breakfast earlier.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: What was dinner like at home too? When you got home from school.

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Oh, when we got home from school, sometimes it was stew or soup, you know. And mom would have all kinds of vegetables in it, you know, and then either rice or noodles or macaroni. You know, us could smell that now at the end of the woods. And then that didn't take us long to get home. From then on, you know, we'd have our big bowls and then knock two off crackers. But she always had home made bread. It smells good to me just now. That was just, it just seemed like that was the greatest time in my fellas life. You know, rushing home and tank up.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Did you have a whole wheat cereal lunch? Would you eat that much?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Well, mom would cook whole wheat lots of times.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Was that for breakfast?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: No, well, sometimes we'd have them for breakfast. You know, she would cook it during the day and then we'd have a bowl of it with sugar and milk before we went to bed. Or sometimes she'd have to leave it on the heater stove and it would be ready to get into it in the morning too. And I still like that. That was a good way of doing it.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: And what did your father do for a living?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Well, when we first moved from up there, he went back to Spain with the old farmers that he had farmed for, you know. And we were alone up there, mom and us kids. And then he got work on the section and then he got the boss of it, so he just, of the crew. So he just stayed there until he retired.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: How long was the day when he worked? How long did he be gone?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: He just had an eight hour day. In the wintertime it was different. He usually takes a train in Princeton and right up the track to the end of these lines. And then walked back down the road, peeling out switches, you know, when the snow was on, stuff like that. That was hard when he got home, you know. Sometimes he'd take the car, you know.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Oh, the carton.

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: He always hardly made it. But that was just a lot of kids. To feed the children.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Did you use to tan your hides at all? The beak hides or anything? Would you give them or sell them to someone or did they just get tossed in the hides?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: I don't know. I can't remember as a little kid, but in life you never say so though.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Did your father hunt much?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: No… no, he never did shoot again.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Was he against shooting here?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Well, when the boys got older, the young boys got older, they used to hunt. But my dad, he didn't and I don't know why. He was just anti that way. But he liked the me and the boys got it, I know. Maybe he can have a better life than that. And I know he did one time because Hawks used to bother the chiefs of that. And I shot one one time. He climbed upon a log and stood up there so smart and crazy. I got him but it knocked me down off the log. Back down on the ground. That wasn't funny.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: How far out of Harvard did you live?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: A mile from Harvard. The store. The post office.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Which one?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: It would be North. I think it was where the old schoolhouse was and then just straight up three-quarters of a mile up this road. And it was never hard to walk to school or anything. Sometimes I'm bad because there's so much snow. And the frost would freeze and make a crust. And that was when it was fun. Keep off our boots. We didn't have to wear them. And then we'd get to scoot down to school and start trotting at home. Because then we'd go down the flat. We didn't have to stick up the hilly road up there.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Did you go to dances? Did all the kids troop together?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: I think they had the one with the piano. Ruby, again, played the piano. She was one of the ones that did. And then they had a violin. Maybe sometimes drums. And they had a dance on Friday night. Oh man, they were fun. But that took us.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Would your mom stay at home?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Most of the time she did. He'd take us down and I didn't see that we'd get home. So they thought we was old enough to... And that was... He used to let us go with the boys then when we got older. The last times he'd show up to dance to see that we did it ourselves. I mean, you know, he didn't like to go to a dance and then run outdoors or anything else. We went to the dance and was supposed to stay in the building. And oftentimes popped up around there to see that we did. Of course we didn't ever walk in either. To leave the hall. Because you'd hear people talking about others who did, so... Seems like a long time ago. But yet awfully short time too.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Were things stricter than you think?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: I think that it was because maybe there was just times when there was something else… hi.

segments.speaker: Unknown Speaker
segments.words: How are you?

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Just fine.

segments.speaker: Unknown Speaker
segments.words: Good.

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: Now this is my son's wife. My daughter-in-law. And this is Mrs. Sam.

segments.speaker: Laura Schrager
segments.words: Schrager. Laura Schrager.

segments.speaker: Unknown Speaker
segments.words: Oh, hi.

segments.speaker: Anna Utt
segments.words: And right now she's taking me. So turn her off.
